candidate.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — tracheostomy airway emergency preparedness
candidate.educational_objective: Maintain immediate bedside access to essential tracheostomy emergency equipment, including a replacement tube, obturator, bag-valve-mask device, and suction setup, so airway patency and ventilation can be rapidly supported if the tracheostomy becomes obstructed or displaced.

options.A: A replacement tracheostomy tube, an obturator, a bag-valve-mask device, and a suction catheter setup
options.B: A pulse oximeter, stethoscope, and oxygen tubing, with replacement airway equipment stored on the unit
options.C: A spare tracheostomy tube of the same size and tracheostomy ties, without a bag-valve-mask or suction setup
options.D: An oral airway and incentive spirometer, with tracheostomy replacement equipment brought only if decannulation occurs

candidate.rationale: NCBI Nursing Skills states that a replacement tracheostomy tube, an obturator, a bag-valve-mask device, and a suction catheter kit must be available in the room for patient safety. The same chapter also specifies bedside access to the obturator, spare tracheostomy tubes including the same size and one size smaller, and a bag-valve-mask device. Therefore A is the best answer. Monitoring equipment alone does not replace airway-rescue equipment; a same-size spare tube without ventilation and suction capability is incomplete; and oral-airway/incentive-spirometry equipment does not address an acute tracheostomy airway emergency.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Acute-care tracheostomy patients require immediately available airway-rescue equipment including a replacement tracheostomy tube, obturator, bag-valve-mask device, and suction equipment; the chapter also specifies same-size and one-size-smaller spare tubes.
